nameStory: Blackthorn gets its name from its extremely dark, almost black bark and its fearsome thorns that can pierce right through clothing. The fruit is called a 'sloe,' which comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'blue-black,' perfectly describing these dusky little plums that pucker your mouth.
description: Blackthorn is a thorny shrub or small tree that forms dense, impenetrable thickets. This European native occasionally shows up in New England, growing 6-15 feet tall with a spreading, tangled growth habit. It's covered in sharp spines and produces small white flowers in early spring, followed by blue-black fruits that are extremely tart. The dark bark and zigzag branching pattern make it distinctive even in winter.

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Numerous sharp, straight spines up to 2 inches long emerge directly from the branches - these aren't just pointed twigs but true thorns that feel rock-hard and can easily puncture skin

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white flowers with 5 petals appear in early spring before the leaves emerge, covering the thorny branches like snow - they have a faint almond-like fragrance

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Round blue-black fruits about the size of large blueberries ripen in fall and taste extremely sour and astringent, leaving your mouth dry and puckered

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark brown to nearly black bark feels rough and becomes deeply furrowed with age, contrasting sharply with the white flowers in spring

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, thorny thickets through underground suckers, creating nearly impenetrable masses of tangled, spiny branches

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves with finely toothed edges feel smooth and are arranged alternately along the branches, emerging after the flowers fade

habitat: In New England, blackthorn is rarely found but may occur in old farmsteads, abandoned properties, or areas where it was once cultivated. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate poor, rocky conditions. Look for it along field edges, old stone walls, or in disturbed areas where European plants have naturalized.

seasonality.spring: Dense clusters of small white flowers bloom in April before leaves appear, creating spectacular thorny bouquets that smell faintly of almonds.
seasonality.summer: Green leaves are fully developed and small green fruits begin forming, while the thorny branches create nearly impenetrable thickets.
seasonality.fall: Blue-black sloe fruits ripen and become extremely tart, while leaves may turn yellow before dropping.
seasonality.winter: Bare thorny branches with dark bark and persistent dried fruits make identification possible, along with the characteristic dense, tangled growth pattern.

funFact: The fruits are so mouth-puckeringly sour they're inedible raw, but in Britain they're the key ingredient in sloe gin - the alcohol mellows their harsh tannins into a sweet, almond-flavored liqueur that takes months to properly mature.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other thorny shrubs like hawthorn, but blackthorn's thorns are straight spikes growing directly from branches, while hawthorn has branched thorns and different leaf shapes. Remember: blackthorn = black bark and straight spikes.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'blackthorn,' it's actually a type of wild plum, not related to true thorns at all. This European species is extremely rare in New England with only 8 recorded observations, so finding one would be quite special for botanists.
compareHints: Unlike its common Prunus relatives like chokecherry and black cherry, blackthorn is heavily armed with long, sharp thorns and stays shrub-sized rather than becoming a tree. Its flowers appear before the leaves (unlike most cherries), and the fruits are much more astringent than other wild plums and cherries in our area.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's wild cherries, black cherry stands out by growing into a large tree with distinctively scaly bark.
Among New England's native cherries, chokecherry is distinguished by its upright flower clusters and tendency to form thickets.
Unlike its Prunus relatives, beach plum stays low and shrubby rather than growing into trees like black cherry or chokecherry.
Fire cherry differs from its cousin black cherry by being much smaller in stature and having narrower leaves, plus its flowers bloom in flat clusters rather than long drooping racemes.
Wild cherry stands out from its Prunus relatives by its distinctive peeling bark and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's wild cherries, sand cherry is unique for its low, spreading habit – all the others (black cherry, chokecherry, fire cherry) grow as upright trees or tall shrubs.
Unlike tall cherries like black cherry or chokecherry that grow as trees, Susquehanna Sandcherry stays low and shrubby.
Among its Prunus relatives, Canada plum stands out with its distinctively dark bark - much darker than American plum or any of the cherries.
Peach trees are smaller and shorter-lived than most of their Prunus relatives in New England.
Unlike cherries in the same genus, American plum has larger, rounder fruits that don't grow in hanging clusters, and the fruits have the characteristic plum 'seam' running along one side.
Compared to native American plums, domestic plums produce larger, less tart fruits and grow into taller trees.
Among its Prunus relatives, sour cherry is distinguished by its small size and weeping growth habit - most other cherries in New England grow much taller and more upright.
Bird cherry stands out from other New England Prunus species by its long, drooping flower clusters that appear after leaf-out, unlike our native cherries which bloom before or with emerging leaves.
Unlike native cherries which have clusters of flowers, cherry-plum flowers appear more individually along branches.

Unlike our native black cherry which has white flowers in long clusters and darker, scaly bark, North Japanese hill cherry has pink flowers in shorter, drooping clusters and smooth, glossy reddish bark.
Unlike native New England Prunus species like wild cherry or chokecherry which grow as large trees, flowering almond stays shrub-sized and is clearly ornamental.
Among the Prunus species in New England, Nanking Cherry is unique for its consistently shrubby growth habit and fuzzy leaves.
